title: The Sunday Papers
summary:
While following a peculiar trail of silver and saffron leaves around the largest roots of the Treehouse, you come across a hexagonal wooden door lying half-hidden among ivy and moss. Scraping away the dirt, you discover a faint, absurd engraving of a newspaper. What mystery is here? You turn the brass knob – strange, it is warm! – and the engraving of the newspaper flutters. The pages turn faster and faster, emitting a howling gale that bowls you head over foot. When you pick yourself up, you are inside a vast attic full of books and bricabrac, lit from one side by windows that offer no view of the outside world – just light and mist.

Tarnation! You have been lured into the eternal prison of Sunday Afternoon. Fortunately, there are several ways to escape. Each of the arcane objects before you is secretly a portal, transporting you to another site of arcane activity, in a bizarre web of diversions that cannot possibly reflect the hand of a human curator. Which will you choose?

title: How Origame Digital are channelling and defacing Lovecraft over a trilogy of "inherently indigenous" anti-fascist games

Lovecraft novella it alternately riffs on and skewers, Penguin Colony takes you to an ancient alien city of crabby cuboid geometry and helical designs – comparable at a glance to Lovecraft's "terraces of every sort of provocative disproportion", but here given strangely everyday, anachronistic-seeming labels, such as "Downtown". Later, you're shown flashes of footage of the streets of Melbourne in Australia - developer Origame Digital's base of operations, and a city built on stolen Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung and Bunurong Boon Wurrung land.

When I first set foot in Downtown, in the unassuming body of a Rockhopper penguin, I thought the broad idea was to satirically redefine modern settlements built by European colonisers as Lovecraftian relics, intrusions from the cosmic beyond. This irony seems most pointed in sections where you steer a group of M&amacrori characters, journeying south to prevent an expedition of German and British Nazi occultists from resurrecting a surviving elder being they call the "one true Aryan king". title: There were 47 graphics chip makers in 1998. Where did they all go?
summary:
Some may find this hard to believe, given the absolute state of the market today, but if you were building a gaming PC in 1998, the hard part wasn’t finding somewhere that had 3D cards in stock for a reasonable price. It was choosing the right one among a glut of potential, reasonably affordable options.

In 1998, 47 companies were designing or selling PC graphics, driving a market that hit 130 million units and outsold PCs themselves. Just two years later, at the turn of the new millennium, only 15 remained, and not long after that, there were merely two: Nvidia and ATI, nowadays part of AMD.

title: Keeping hold of Company of Heroes was essential for Relic to leave Sega, Relic CEO says – "Without it we would have been a dead studio"
summary:

Responsible for lauded RTS series Homeworld, Dawn of War, and Company of Heroes, they also dabbled in other genres with third-person shooter The Outfit and the original Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine. Yet, despite this history, in 2024, when Relic were negotiating their sale from Sega to UK investment firm Emona Capita, CEO Justin Dowdeswell knew the rights to Company of Heroes had to be part of the deal. "Without it we would have been a dead studio," he tells me.

Without naming names Dowdeswell points out that there are "numerous examples" of studios that weren't able to survive on their name alone. Not only did Relic need the ability to make more games in the series that they were known for, but they also needed the income from back catalogue sales a series like Company of Heroes provides.

title: All Hail Blood Gulch, Halo’s Greatest Multiplayer Map
summary:
After 25 years, Halo can be remembered for many things. It's among the best launch games of all time, which was pivotal in making Xbox a serious console contender. Its campaign was so brilliantly designed, from set pieces like The Silent Cartographer to the distinct and believable AI behaviors, that it was one of the few games at the time that compelled me to replay on its hardest difficulty.

But perhaps what has made it so meaningful and memorable over the years--which is sadly absent from the recent Halo: Campaign Evolved--is its competitive multiplayer. And I can't really think about Halo multiplayer without thinking of Blood Gulch, especially when it was essentially the only map I would ever play with friends.

Multiplayer sessions fixated on just one map was a bit of a common occurrence among my friends, given the countless sleepovers that involved GoldenEye on the N64 and doing nothing but having shootouts in the toilets of Facility. In comparison, Halo took a while to make an imprint for us, considering that I had to wait until the following Christmas after its launch before I could get an Xbox.

I was also the only person among my friends to own Microsoft's console, but Halo's influence would spread like The Flood when I introduced it to my friend Josh. We had gone to different schools in sixth form but stayed in touch as I was going to church back then, so it became a ritual that after evening service, he would come around to my place to work through Halo's campaign in co-op. By the end of its explosive final mission, he was converted and got his own Xbox.

It was also at this point where we were able to meaningfully experience Halo's multiplayer. After all, shooting at each other in 1v1 matches was a bit one-note, but Josh also had younger brothers, so suddenly I was going over to his house with spare controllers so we could play four-player splits-screen just like the N64 days. This was when we got our introduction to Blood Gulch, a name I had only been able to read about for months, but would become permanently etched from thereon.

On the face of it, Blood Gulch is the antithesis of a typical FPS map, its canyon design giving too much space in a genre that's often more fast-paced, with fewer tactical corners to poke around. However, the open field was also what made it viable for vehicular action, letting you rampage with your pal on a Warthog or run someone over with a Ghost. But when thinking of its semi-symmetrical layout with a base at each end, it also brings to mind a large football field, which also leads me to Capture the Flag.

Halo may not have invented this mode, but as a console gamer first, it was my real introduction to it, and felt transformative. While in the days of GoldenEye we would quite happily run around shooting each other, now we actually had a concrete goal to work towardr as a team, which also didn't feel completely different from the attack and defense of five-a-side football.

Even so, there's only so much potential you can wring out of 2v2 CTF, with one side haplessly carrying the flag while the other tries to fight off the opposing Spartans, and we occasionally made things harder on ourselves by turning off vehicles. 

The bigger game changer was discovering the System Link Cable that allowed us to connect multiple Xbox consoles together, which was how I got my first taste of a LAN party. I could also count on Josh to evangelize on Halo's behalf so that we ended up roping in enough folks from church to get together for 4v4 matches (this was still only half of its full potential, as it was actually possible to connect up to four Xbox systems for 16-player multiplayer).

It was via this method that we really got to appreciate the balanced yet asymmetrical design of Blood Gulch, such as how the Red team has access to a ridge that's a perfect sniping spot, while the Blue team is closer to a tunnel system, though that doesn't prevent each team from taking advantage of either route. The base would be at one moment a quiet place to shoot banter with another defending teammate before exploding into tight shootouts when someone tried to make a scramble for the flag.

I've played many more team-based FPS games over the years too, but few ever have as as memorable a moments ascatching the glint of a sniper hiding behind Sniper's Rock and then trying to sneak your way up to take them out first, the foolhardy derring-do of stealing a flag while praying your invisibility power-up lasts, or having everyone pile into a Scorpion tank and going in loud. 

Given the setup required, I would be lying if I said I got to experience Halo via System Link more than a handful of times. After all, the first time we managed to organize this event was the summer before I went away to university, where I was back to being the only person in my immediate circle who was gaming, let alone an Xbox owner. Of course, the year Halo 2 came out and I was back for the holidays, we naturally wrangled people together again to link up and load up its Blood Gulch remake, Coagulation, taking to the new additions like energy swords and Banshees even if they might have upset its predecessor's balance. It's the seemingly all-night-long sessions at Blood Gulch that are so burned into my memory.

I don't think I'm alone in that, given the map's popularity over the years, having not only been remade by Bungie in subsequent entries, but even by the community the moment the Forge update was added to Halo Infinite. In later years, its beloved status has found it being remade in other shooters, including CS:GO and Fortnite. But beyond the genre, its cultdom was arguably cemented by the web series Red vs. Blue, its creator Burnie Burns perfectly tapping into its desolate desert as a space for contemplating existentialist themes on almost the same level as a Samuel Beckett play. 

But for all the ways that Halo has evolved over the years, for me it was Halo: The Master Chief Collection getting a System Link update in 2018 that was the most meaningful. Over that time, I had stopped going to church and even spent many years a lapsed gamer, but once the habit had kicked back in, I had also gotten back in touch with Josh. While we had caught up with various online multiplayer games, such as Destiny and Overwatch, the opportunity to relive Halo LAN parties 15 years later was something we just had to seize.

Of course, we had all gotten older with more responsibilities and busy schedules, but there was something special about how despite the different paths we'd taken, Halo somehow brought us back together for one night, albeit with each team huddling around a larger and sharper monitor than the CRT TVs we made do with back in the day. And despite Halo MCC including the new Bloodlines map--a remake of Coagulation--when it came to setting up a Capture the Flag session, there was no question that Blood Gulch was our unanimous pick as a pure nostalgia hit.

Halo may feel like a shadow of its former self these days, its recent campaign remake feeling more like a pristine eulogy than a path toward the future, which will now be under the direction of Activision.

But no matter how bleak or uncertain that future looks, at least we'll always have Blood Gulch.

title: I Loved My Xbox 360s–All Four Of Them
summary:
Xbox is celebrating its 25-year anniversary today, November 15, 2026. Below, we take a look back at Microsoft's great, and infamously buggy, second console.

In the mid to late aughts, the Xbox 360 reigned supreme. It felt like the center of the gaming universe, as the best place to play multiplatform hits like Modern Warfare and Grand Theft Auto, and the only way to play exclusive blockbusters like Halo 3. All of my high school friends were on Xbox Live every night, and online gaming became a ritual to me. My clearest, purest memories of gaming come from this era, and the Xbox 360 remains one of my favorite consoles of all time. It’s too bad that I burned through so many of them.

The Xbox 360 was as infamous for hardware failures as it was famous for its amazing software library. It’s nearly impossible to look back at the 360 without also recalling the Red Ring of Death, the ominous three red lights surrounding the power button that indicates a general hardware error. This red ring was a plague on the initial Xbox 360 model, and the shipping and repairs for affected consoles cost Microsoft a little over a billion dollars. The Xbox 360 platform as a whole had an amazing lifespan--the first Xbox 360 consoles themselves, though, did not.

Somehow, I had completely avoided the dreaded red ring with my original 360 model, but it wasn’t spared of all technical issues. One night, I plopped my Halo 3 disc in the tray, only to be met with a suspicious clicking-like noise. Instead of the Halo 3 icon appearing on my dashboard, a generic “Open Tray” message appeared in its place. Troubleshooting was a maddening process--all of my discs were returning the same message, and Google searches were largely unhelpful. Despite the functioning software, my 360 refused to read any of my physical games. It quickly became clear that my 360 was a lemon.

I removed the hard drive, enveloped my 360 in bubble wrap, stuffed it in a box, and left it with UPS. The ordeal cost me $90, as my Xbox was out of warranty. My precious Xbox 360 and the digital space that my friends occupied on a nightly basis became completely out of reach.

About two weeks later, my replacement 360 came home. Being able to jump back into Xbox Live felt like rejoining society, and the countless hours of Halo, Call of Duty, and Left 4 Dead resumed. 

Months later, the clicking noise returned, and I was back to square one. Back to UPS for me. It felt like cruel irony that my consoles never received the ominous red ring, yet fatal errors still caught up with them anyway. My third Xbox 360 fared well, I recall.

Then, after leaks and rumors, Microsoft announced and shadow-dropped the slim Xbox 360. For me, and presumably many others who went through similar hardware struggles, this announcement was a godsend. The Xbox 360 was a fantastic platform with limitless entertainment, but it was unfortunately trapped in a sickened body. This new, sleeker model was a total overhaul of its internals and form factor, and it was incapable of red-ringing (mainly because it literally had no red LEDs). You can bet that I was quick to trade in my original model 360 for this newfangled, glossy Xbox.

It only took nearly half a decade, but Microsoft finally fixed its biggest problem. The Xbox 360 platform overcame its flawed engineering, and the hardware itself was finally able to keep up with the amazing software support and bustling online community that had built up despite all of the technical issues. I don’t remember any issues with my slim Xbox 360 in the years that followed (except accidentally hitting that touch-sensitive power button every once in a while), and that version of the Xbox 360 is how I choose to remember it today.

Arguably, no platform since then has had the omnipresence of the Xbox 360, at least in the West. Despite the popularity and sales success of the PlayStation 4 and the Nintendo Switch, it felt as if the Xbox 360 dominated attention and broke the containment of gaming communities into the mainstream in ways other platforms couldn’t. It was a transformative platform, defining what an online service infrastructure should look like for gaming, and housing so many influential titles like Gears of War, Mass Effect, The Elder Scrolls 4, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare, BioShock, and Grand Theft Auto 4.

For me, the Xbox 360 was a source of joy, and the time of the platform’s peak was when gaming became a central pillar of my life. But with all of its successes, the 360’s prolific technical fiascos are forever intertwined with the platform’s history. They say you have to break a few eggs to make an omelette--I apparently had to break at least two Xboxes before I could truly have fun.

title: GTA 6 Is Like The Olympics – “A Rare Cultural Moment” With Massive Ripple Effects
summary:
After years of development, multiple delays, and what can only be assumed to be one of the biggest production budgets ever, Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on November 19. The game is poised to "blot out the sun," some experts believe, and its release looms so large that other gaming companies are shifting dates for their own games to stay out of the blast radius. 

Francis Lawrence, the director of the new Hunger Games movie Sunrise on the Reaping, which comes out a day after GTA 6, has said he hopes people can find the time to play the game and watch his movie. In short, GTA 6 is seen by some as a black hole that will suck up time, attention, and money from the broader gaming economy--and even workplaces, as people dive into the 80-hour game they've been waiting a decade to play. 

To help make sense of, and contextualize, the enormity of GTA 6's looming launch, GameSpot caught up with Bart Spiegel of the global professional services and research company PricewaterhouseCoopers, or PwC. He told GameSpot that GTA 6 is "something much bigger than a traditional entertainment launch," and is more akin to an event like the Olympics.

He believes GTA 6 is a "rare cultural moment" that "commands extraordinary attention and creates economic activity well beyond the event itself."

Spiegel said he foresees potential shifts beyond gaming, in places like TV viewership, music consumption, social media engagement, and even travel. "In an increasingly fragmented entertainment landscape, it's rare for a single release to command this much attention across so many industries simultaneously. That's what makes this moment so significant," he said.

An economics professor recently claimed that about 1.5 million people plan to "call out sick" to play GTA 6, and this could come at a "cost" of $1 billion to the US economy. Spiegel said people should remember that GTA 6 isn't anything new or special as it relates to taking time off work. "People regularly plan time off around major cultural and entertainment events, and this is another example of consumers prioritizing an experience they're excited about," he said.

That being said, Spiegel remarked that PwC has observed estimates suggesting time-off requests near GTA 6's release could be 9% to 17% higher than normal. "But what's more interesting to me is what happens outside the workplace. If millions of people are spending additional hours gaming, they're potentially spending less time watching television, going out to restaurants, or engaging in other activities," he said.

"And unlike a sporting event that lasts a few hours or a few weeks, this experience could keep people engaged for months. So the broader economic implications may extend well beyond a single day of missed work," he added.

"Huge net positive"

GTA 6 is expected to be an enormous success commercially--it's reportedly already sold 11 million units through pre-purchases, and that could rise to 25 million at launch. That would work out to $2 billion in revenue, which would cover the game's entire development budget and most of its marketing spend, Sensor Tower said. But many are also saying that GTA 6 represents the last of a dying breed, and that other publishers might learn all the wrong lessons from its success. Spiegel said GTA 6 is going to be a "huge net positive for the gaming industry as a whole," in part because its success will reiterate to the broader entertainment and media landscape that games are culturally significant. At the same time, Spiegel said he doesn't foresee a world in which other publishers try to replicate a blockbuster of this magnitude. 

"Very few organizations have the capital, expertise, and intellectual property required to support investments on this scale. These are extraordinary events, not necessarily repeatable business models," Spiegel said. 

If GTA 6 is the huge success it's projected to be, it could positively uplift the broader gaming ecosystem in a lot of ways, Spiegel continued. 

"It could attract new audiences, renew investor interest, and create opportunities across advertising, payments, technology, and content creation. The real lesson isn't that everyone needs to build the next billion-dollar game. It's that gaming is an increasingly powerful part of the entertainment economy, with opportunities that extend well beyond the games themselves," he said.

Some companies, like Ubisoft, see GTA 6 not as something to be strictly afraid of. CEO Yves Guillemot says, that's because the rising tide that is GTA 6 could help drive more people to gaming overall. In fact, Ubisoft is putting out a big new update for one of its biggest games, Rainbow Six Siege, right around GTA 6's launch.

Mat Piscatella of Circana reminded people that not everyone wants to play GTA 6, and he pushed back against the theory that it's a bad business idea to launch a game near GTA 6.

"The fear of many teams to put their game in the same window as GTA is completely overblown. GTA is going to be a massive game. Of course it is. It’s going to be a huge cultural event, but not every one of the 49 million people who own a PS5 or an Xbox Series in the US is going to be interested in that," he told GamesBeat.

Could GTA 6 lead the push to more in-game ads?

Spiegel went on to say that one additional follow-on effect from GTA 6 could be something that gamers might balk at but publishers and investors might salivate over. He said that if GTA 6 succeeds in the way people expect it to, and draw people into its world for tens--or even hundreds--of hours, that could demonstrate to the wider market that it's time for gaming, as an industry, to do more with advertising. 

"When millions of people are spending substantial amounts of time in interactive entertainment environments, it's natural for advertisers and investors to consider how they might participate," he said. 

Advertising for mobile and social games is already commonplace, but it's less present in the PC and console gaming market. There are examples, of course, as companies have already undertaken efforts to put ads into gaming with mixed results. Gamers quickly revolted when EA put ads in a UFC game, prompting EA to pull them quickly to help quell the backlash. Despite that, EA recently announced the formation of a new EA Advertising division that will seek to put ads "directly into gameplay." That announcement didn't go over well, either, as fans pushed back against the idea of having to see ads in yet another place in their life. Other examples have been received more positively, or at least ambivalently, with a trucking company buying ad space in the American Truck Simulator series to help recruit staff. 

Xbox, for its part, has big plans to put more ads in gaming. Xbox CSO Matthew Ball said advertising in console games could help with the "two-sided problem" that AAA gaming faces today. Development costs keep going up and up, and Ball said ads--as long as they're not overly in-your-face--could be a way to help developers make more money and solidify their business fundamentals. Of course, if these companies insert more ads into gaming, that doesn't mean they'll stop hawking things like DLC, microtransactions, and battle passes; they'll likely both happen in concert. As Spiegel sees it, though, if executed correctly, advertising could be a big boon for gaming.

"What's particularly interesting is that the opportunity extends beyond placing advertisements inside games. There's an entire ecosystem of digital advertising infrastructure, technology, and services that could benefit as gaming continues to grow. I expect we'll see increasing interest in those opportunities, particularly from investors looking for exposure to gaming without taking on the considerable financial risks associated with developing blockbuster titles," he said.

More investment

During the COVID years, the gaming industry saw massive revenue and player growth as people, forced to stay inside due to stay-at-home orders, turned to games to pass the time, have fun, and connect with friends. At the same time, interest rates were historically low. The cost to borrow money was so attractive that publishers ramped up significantly. 

The COVID-era boost to gaming did not last, though, and the industry is now challenged, to say the least, with numerous developers cutting staff, cancelling projects, and scaling back in other ways. If GTA 6 is indeed a massive success, it could trigger renewed interest in gaming as an investment vehicle, Spiegel believes, but not necessarily exclusively for funding new games and studios. Instead, Spiegel said he foresees big investment growth for discrete elements of gaming, including advertising, payment services, and AI buildouts.

"I absolutely think a release of this magnitude will get the attention of investors, corporate executives, and private equity firms. But I don't necessarily think that translates into another wave of billion-dollar game development," he said. "The economics of producing games at this scale are incredibly challenging, and very few organizations have the resources, expertise, and intellectual property necessary to justify those investments."

"Instead, I think investors will increasingly ask how they can participate in the broader gaming ecosystem," Spiegel added. "That could mean opportunities in advertising, payment infrastructure, technology services, mobile gaming, or artificial intelligence applications that support game development."

On the subject of AI, Spiegel said he believes it's a "particularly interesting variable" because it could, at least in theory, allow developers to work more efficiently and bring down costs. There is debate about whether or not this is a genuine reality or wishful thinking on the part of AI companies trying to sell their products and services. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, for example, recently told Business Insider that, despite Take-Two adopting AI products for some of its workflows, the company has not seen a material decrease in its cost structure. In fact, many theorize that AI-supported workflows will only make work more intense. For his part, Spiegel said AI in game development remains only an "emerging opportunity rather than a guaranteed outcome."

"The longer-term impact may be less about creating another generation of massive blockbusters and more about directing investment toward the businesses and technologies that support the gaming economy," he said. 

Who should be afraid?

A lot has already been said and written about publishers moving their release dates to avoid GTA 6, and Spiegel said he foresees dramatic possibilities for how GTA 6 could take the wind out of the sails of other entertainment near its launch. He said GTA 6 is not just a major gaming launch. Instead, he thinks it's an "event that could temporarily reshape how millions of consumers spend their time and money."

"Streaming could be particularly vulnerable. Every hour someone spends gaming is potentially an hour they're not watching a television show or movie. And because this launch falls just before the holiday season, it could make it difficult for streaming services to match the exceptionally strong viewership numbers we saw last year," he said.

Movie theaters could be tested, Spiegel said, and one highly anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, will be one to watch in particular. It comes to theaters on Friday, November 20, which is one day after GTA 6 releases. Director Francis Lawrence said he hopes fans find the time to play GTA 6 and go see his movie, but it remains to be seen what effect, if any, GTA 6's release will have on that film's performance at the box office. Spiegel said movie studios are banking on the belief that the theatrical experience "offers something consumers can't get from their living rooms." 

There is a Thursday Night Football game happening on the same day that GTA 6 releases, with the Indianapolis Colts taking on the Houston Texans. Spiegel said the live-sports category overall could be "more resilient" because of its nature as an event happening live that fans of those teams, or fans of the NFL in general, feel compelled to watch live as it happens. A movie or TV show, meanwhile, is on-demand entertainment. 

GTA 6 is a hugely anticipated release, and it's poised to bring lapsed gamers back into the fold, but anyone who doesn't already have a PS5 or Xbox Series X|S should prepare themselves for sticker shock. That's because, for a variety of reasons, new consoles today are actually hundreds of dollars more expensive than they were when they launched in 2020.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has frankly acknowledged, "The rising cost of hardware is not a good thing." At the same time, Zelnick isn't shaking in his boots about what this means for GTA 6. He thinks GTA 6 will be so good and so compelling that people will buy in no matter what.

"I don’t think it will slow us down any because, you know, we’re delivering, we believe we’re delivering experiences that people want,” Zelnick said. “However, a lower price point for hardware would be a good thing because there’d be more hardware in people’s hands."

Who benefits?

In terms of companies, products, people, and services that could benefit from the ripple effects of GTA 6's release, Spiegel said music associated with the game could surge in listening activity. This has already happened, as streams of Tom Petty's "Love Is A Long Road" surged after the first trailer for GTA 6 used the song back in 2023. More recently, Cliff Richard's 1976 hit "Devil Woman" showed up in the GTA 6 Extended Look on Netflix, helping the song reach more people, including young people who maybe never even knew about the song. Spiegel said social media platforms could benefit from GTA 6's release as well, thanks to fans uploading gameplay clips, livestreams, and other forms of user-generated content inspired by GTA 6. Beyond this, the world of food delivery could see an uptick in activity as people opt to stay in to play GTA 6 (while in-person restaurants and other nightlife venues could take a hit). 

"The broader point is that the impact could extend into parts of the economy we don't traditionally associate with gaming," Spiegel said. "For business leaders, the question is whether they're competing with this cultural moment for consumer attention or finding ways to participate in it. That's what makes this launch so much more interesting than simply tracking how many copies are sold."

title: Casualties: Unknown Is A Brutal 97%-Rated Survival Game That Will Make You Realize Your Mortality, And At A Cheap Price, Too
summary:
There’s no light. The shuttle that brought me into the depths is fitted with just a shower, and the darkness swallows everything around me. Each step is as painful as the last, like walking barefoot on LEGO bricks, as I narrowly miss traps. Corpses are frozen as I head further down, a reminder of who came before and likely what I’ll end up as. I crack the glass of a small base, crawling through to gain access, shrapnel filling my foot as I sneak through. Infection rises, but with no medicine, it spreads. It gets worse. It gets worse. I die.

That was my first run of Casualties: Unknown. I’ve played a lot of survival games, but few are as brutal, as dark, and as thrilling as this Steam game, which has earned the ‘Overwhelmingly Positive’ badge of approval from almost 2,000 reviews, giving it a 97% rating and making it an indie gem. It’s easy to look at its various mechanics and think it sounds challenging, masochistic, and downright terrifying, and those are all accurate. It’s also a game about hope and getting through the hardest times, pushing yourself to become stronger and better.

Let me explain: Casualties sees you play as an ‘Experiment’, the affectionate name given to creatures spliced with human and animal DNA. On an alien planet, your job is to push further into the depths, scavenging alien flora and fauna to craft resources and eventually getting deeper and deeper. However, what makes Casualties so hard is that it has a fully simulated injury and cardiovascular system; one wrong move could leave you dealing with an open wound and nothing to patch it up with.

Every run is as customizable as you’d like. You could make it ridiculously easy, albeit still with some challenge, or you could make it a dreadful experience—it’s entirely up to you. Death is practically inevitable, especially when you’re starting out, but each step you take in subsequent runs builds your knowledge, and eventually, you may even make it to the second layer. There are 11, by the way.

It’s easily one of the best indie games I’ve played, offering a blend of an unforgiving world with a dash of hopeful optimism. And despite just launching, you can grab Casualties: Unknown for just $17.24 / £14.24 at Fanatical. That’s a brilliant launch-day discount, and it easily makes it worth playing, whether it’s out of morbid curiosity or the hope that you’ll eventually beat it.

Good luck, either way.

title: I Love How Music Makes Soulframe Feel Like A Folktale
summary:
Soulframe still isn't out yet, but its Preludes were finally publicly opened on November 6, giving me my first chance to try it out. I was expecting "Warframe but fantasy," and to be fair, a lot of Soulframe is like that, but so much of Digital Extremes' new action-role-playing game feels very different. I'm floored--I've tried to get into Warframe several times and just kept bouncing off of it for one reason or another, but here I am really enjoying Soulframe and trying to figure out which live-service game I'm going to have to retire from to put Soulframe into my regular rotation. And it's really all because of the game's music.

Admittedly, music is one of the best parts about Warframe too. While I've never been able to really get into it, the reason I kept trying Warframe is because I'd keep hearing these absolute awesome sea shanties and vocal-led orchestral scores and thinking, "I want to play a game that sounds like that." But I never knew how to get to any of those moments to hear them play out in game. 

I tried getting into Warframe way too late, when the game had already transformed into something that largely catered to the players who were already in the ecosystem. The game just felt way too big of a beast to tackle as a newbie. Which is fine! That happens to every live-service game eventually.

Soulframe is new so it doesn't have that problem yet. And even if it did, it feels like it incorporates its music way more regularly and meaningfully than Warframe seems to. Almost every aspect of Soulframe (so far) is shaped around its music, including its poetry, birdsong, choral folktales, and orchestral scores. Character creation is writing a poem about how beautiful your mother was, several characters communicate solely in sing-song rhyme, and the first storyline revolves around learning the song that will not only play during the climatic boss battle but will also be played by your character in order to finally cleanse the evil you're fighting. 

In Soulframe, music is just implemented everywhere. It feels like a story that's meant to be listened to, like a folktale, and you just happen to be playing through it instead. The vibe is not dissimilar to games like South of Midnight or Kena: Bridge of Spirits.

I haven't experienced anything in terms of the gameplay that has wowed me thus far, but it's a solid baseline. It often feels like playing Dragon Age: Inquisition, so if you're like me and mourning the idea we'll never get another one of those, then Soulframe is surprisingly healing. 

At the start, you pick whether you want to strike enemies with a sword, be sneaky with daggers and a bow, or pepper foes with arcane pellets launched from your magical staff. Each of these roles has special abilities that work on a cooldown, and all classes can normally attack, defend, dodge, or jump. The semi-open world is broken up into several explorable sections populated with enemies that have a number above their head denoting whether you can take on a particular group or not, and as you complete side quests and main missions, you'll level up and be able to unlock new skills and equip better armor and weapons.

There's more to the gameplay, like combining certain abilities to take advantage of a staggered enemy or pulling out an enemy's soul to pull off a smite, but it's altogether a very simple loop--the kind you'd normally jump into with a podcast playing in the background so that you can unwind after a stressful day. And I suppose you could still do that here, but you're missing out by muting this game given how so much of the enjoyment comes from how characters talk and how the dynamism of the music causes moments of exploration and combat to flow together, again, like it's all one tale being conveyed. 

Plus, how else would you fully appreciate the pattern-focused rhythm minigames in which you have to play songs to charm animals, relive the memories of a place or person, travel between dimensions, and cleanse the corruption that's hurting a poor magical stag? Get outta here with your silly ocarina or tsuchibue. Soulframe's magical fipple flute is the superior gaming wind instrument!

Soulframe is already shaping up to have a pretty interesting story too. An enchanted melody (I'm telling you, music is everywhere in this game) known as the Spellsong has caused people to forget the importance of nature and the fey and the rites of true magick. But because you are born from an ancient fey lineage, you're able to resist the effects of the brainwashing. Blessed with the powerful song of the courageous Mora, spiritual Iridis, or graceful Saphene, you venture into a land in which humanity has put animals into cages, enslaved beasts with magical armor, and corrupted powerful spirits. 

You're basically a champion of nature, which isn't exactly a novel concept for a fantasy game, but I love how it's portrayed here. You fight humans to free captured animals and fey, destroy the armor of wardogs not to kill them but to free them, and challenge bosses to use the healing power of music to restore their memories of how the world is supposed to be: humanity and nature living side by side. Yeah, it's cheesy, but it feeds into that folktale vibe the rest of the game has going on.

There are certainly plenty of pretty games to look at this year, but Soulframe's Preludes might possess the most arresting sound of any game in 2026. I currently can't stop listening to it, even when I'm not playing the game. So if you're at all like me and have struggled to get into Warframe despite wanting to understand the hype, love a good folktale, or just have never cared about Grand Theft Auto and need something to play in November while everyone else is busy with GTA 6, consider downloading Soulframe. The Preludes are free-to-play, and while what's there is certainly not a full game, what's available feels like the bedrock for something that's going to be excellent.

title: “Physical” GTA 6 Copies Might Be Vulnerable To A Very Stupid But Serious Trick
summary:
Grand Theft Auto 6 ditched traditional discs for its "physical" launch, with Rockstar's game being sold as a digital code-in-box at retailers beginning this week. However, it appears a packaging choice may have accidentally left the game vulnerable to thieves--assuming they have a flashlight.

As shared on the forum ResetEra, users who received a physical version of Grand Theft Auto 6, at least in PEGI regions, report that the game's download code is printed directly on the inside of the cover rather than on a card or separate insert. When a flashlight is focused on the cover from the outside of the closed game case, the download code is visible in reverse.

In other words, there's a serious risk people could go into a store, do this trick, redeem the code, and leave the poor soul who actually buys the game off the shelf without GTA 6.

At this time, the trick does not seem to work on North American copies of GTA 6, as the code is intentionally obscured. Why Rockstar would not use this strategy on all regions is unclear. We've reached out to Rockstar for an explanation and will update this post if and when we receive a response.

If you happen to get your GTA 6 code stolen after paying $80, you can at least sleep soundly knowing that the thief can't play the game yet. Code-in-box copies, as well as digital preorders, all unlock for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S on November 19.

title: GTA 6 Owner Take-Two Is Not Interested In Selling Itself After EA Goes Private For $55 Billion
summary:
Recently, the gaming giant Electronic Arts was taken private in a $55 billion sale to an investor consortium led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. Could GTA 6 owner Take-Two be the next big company that gets acquired? Don't bet on it, CEO Strauss Zelnick says.

Speaking to David Rubenstein, Zelnick said Take-Two's business results have proven that it "can do very well as an independent company."

He said Take-Two's business is already "at scale" and healthy enough financially with a "terrific balance sheet," as he put it.

"We are not in a place where we need to be part of a bigger organization to be competitive. And in the entertainment business, scale matters," he said.

Zelnick said companies that do less than a billion in annual revenue might have issues with developing, marketing, and distributing games at scale. Not only that, but companies that don't generate a lot of money might not be able to survive the realities of the creative business, in which sometimes your product flops.

"But once you're over a billion dollars in annual revenue, and we're way beyond that point. Our guidance is $8 billion to $8.2 billion this fiscal year, additional scale doesn't seem to help you succeed."

In early 2008, Electronic Arts privately pursued a buyout of Take-Two, but after the GTA and BioShock company rejected it, EA went public in an attempt to get a deal done. Later that year, EA abandoned its plans to try to buy Take-Two after the GTA company said it was worth more and EA refused to increase its bid.

In 2019, it was rumored that Sony was attempting to buy Take-Two, but that was ultimately deemed to be unconfirmed market chatter and not a formal bid.

Take-Two has a market cap of more than $42 billion, and that is expected to grow in the year ahead, so it would seemingly take a lot of money to convince Take-Two to sell. Going forward, Zelnick has teased that new GTA games could release even faster, and that could be a positive for the company's financials.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Preloading is underway now, and that's good news because the game has a massive file size.
